The White part on barcodes is what gets scanned. http://www.taltech.com/barcodesoftware/articles/how_barcode_reader_works

Actually, for 1-D barcodes, it's neither the black or white bars that are "scanned". The transition from black-to-white or white-to-black are what is important. The length of time between transitions is what determines the code. The barcodes are symmetrical so that they scan the same way from left-to-right as they do right-to-left. If you pay attention the the width of the black and white bars going from one direction to the other, the widths match. This was done because a code needed to be scanned without regard to its orientation and a "pen" -style reader like the early types could be used in either hand and go left or right. I used to do a lot of work with 1-D barcodes and they are quite ingenious in how they work.
